segments.text: New modeling shows US structural fire losses could nearly triple by 2060 without added protections or climate action. This is Planetterrian Daily, episode 233. Forrests that take in extra sunlight, heat records from two tropical field stations, and a spotlight on nitric oxide particles follow. University of Colorado Boulder researchers at the Cooperative Institute for Research and Environmental Sciences rebuilt a record of fire risk to structures from 1945 through 2023.
history, using historical burned area and housing data as reported by Fizz.org.
They combined that archive with weather, climate and housing density projections and ran
the model out to 2060.
Under a moderate emissions path and no new adaptations, the simulation reaches as many as
449,100 buildings damaged or destroyed.
The largest relative jump and risk sits in the central United States, where grassland fires
are increasing.
In the West, 30% of census tracts facing the steepest risk increases already show high poverty and housing burden.
The paper appears in nature communications, and lead author Virginia Iglesias said in action on climate, construction patterns,
and community involvement will push risk much higher.
She added that eastern fires can be as destructive as western ones, even though communities there have seen fewer such events,
and that Colorado's wildfire resiliency code adopted in July 2025 cannot stand in for
work on social vulnerability.
Pierre Etienne-Banville, a master student in geography at Simon Fraser University, used
an Earth system model to trace climate effects of large-scale forestation that have nothing
to do with carbon dioxide.
Forests absorb more sunlight than grasslands, especially where snow is present, and the warmer
air can hold more water vapor.
When that air crosses oceans, it lifts sea surface temperatures and evaporation, which
then strengthens the greenhouse effect.
Oceans take up the extra heat slowly, so the full remote warming unfolds over centuries,
according to the paper in Earth System Dynamics.
Banville explained that carbon dioxide removal arrives relatively fast as trees grow, while
the non-carbon dioxide warming can lag and cancel part of that cooling.
He said policies for nature-based solutions have to count both time scales if climate
targets are tied to a calendar date.
La Selva in Costa Rica and El Verde in Puerto Rico supplied the long-term station records
for a PLOS climate paper on tropical extremes.
Average temperatures barely moved, yet days above the 95th percentile heat threshold at La
Selva climb from 8 per year to 30 by 2024.
Alonzo Ramirez of North Carolina State University, the lead author, reported that rainfall events
above the 99th percentile at La Selva rose from about 1 per year between 1983 and 1985
to 6 per year in 2024.
El Verde, instead, saw dry days increase from 152 per year to 170.
Co-author Marcelo Ardon, also at NC State, said it was surprising that one site grew wetter
and the other dryer despite their relative proximity.
Ramirez noted that protected tropical research sites were expected to show little change
from human-driven climate shifts, yet both stations recorded changes in climate and ecosystem
function.
Low pressure over Iceland relative to the Azores shifts the jet stream north and steers
storm surges onto northern and central United Kingdom coasts.
Cambridge University scientists pulled 70 years of sea-level records around northwestern
Europe.
up, isolated extreme surge events and used machine learning to group coastlines that
flood together, in work published in the Journal of Geophysical Research Oceans.
The reverse pressure pattern sends the storm south.
Lead author Lizanne Block of Cambridge Earth Sciences found that northern hemisphere and especially
north Atlantic, pressure patterns were the strongest control on where surges land, and that the
links held more clearly across large distances than expected.
She said spotting those Atlantic setups could let forecasters identify which stretches
of coasts should prepare for flooding.
The North Sea's narrow funnel and shallow basin amplify surge height, and storms that
hit southwest England often start off eastern Canada, while those that reach the North Sea
in Scotland often come from off Greenland.
Antarctic strains of the soil bacterium, Arthrobacter, formed genetic lineages that did not appear
in comparison samples from the Attacama Desert, Svalbard or the Tibetan Plateau. The comparison
is published in the proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Authors Carrie A. Walker
and Melody Clark wrote that these organisms evolve solutions to extreme cold,
desiccation, and high ultraviolet B-radiation. Their earlier work cultured bacteria from eight
Antarctic marine invertebrate species and found that two strains slowed growth of epidemic
methamethicillin-resistant staphlococcus aureus,
micro-coccus luteus, and candida albicans in laboratory tests.
Soil temperatures at the collection sites range from 8 degrees Celsius in summer to
below –25 degrees Celsius in winter.
Most people assume that microbes hitchhike so readily on wind and water that the same
lineages appear wherever conditions match.
On the Antarctic continent, the picture is different because long geographic isolation
has let certain bacterial lineages evolve apart from populations on other land masses.
The circumpolar current has kept the continent cut off for 10 to 15 million years,
a span far longer than the roughly one-and-a-half million years the Arctic has been cold,
while remaining connected to surrounding continents. That extended separation
stacked on rapid temperature swings, intense ultraviolet radiation, and scarce nutrients,
patients, favor survival traits that are not required in less isolated cold regions.
Distinct genetic clusters present only in the Antarctic isolates support the idea that
these microbes evolved in place rather than arriving recently from elsewhere.
The same traits that permit life in that setting also appear to produce compounds with medical
interest, including the laboratory inhibition of clinically important resistant pathogens.
A separate investigation around the Rothraer Research Station found that treated wastewater
exerts only limited influence on surrounding marine microbial communities.
Those bacteria readily adapted to warmer temperatures when grown in the lab.
A hint that rising global temperatures could change the conditions that have kept this
uniqueness intact.
These microbes also cycle nutrients and sit at the base of Antarctic food webs.
Documenting which strains exist only on the continent raises practical questions about
conservation priorities, and about the risk of introducing non-native microorganisms through
tourism and scientific operations. University of reading researchers loaded nitric oxide
into organosilica nanoparticles that give off the gas slowly over hours. One hour after
infecting wax moth larvae with skin infection bacteria, they injected the particles. Nine
and ten treated larvae survived three days, compared with roughly six and ten left untreated.
In separate flash tests, the particles cut bacterial counts by four to five orders of magnitude,
and the work appears in the Journal of Drug Delivery Science and Technology.
Lead researcher Vitaly Kutoryanski explained that nitric oxide hits germs on several fronts at once,
which makes resistance harder to evolve, and that the particles solve the problem of storing the gas
and metering it out slowly. Waxmoth larvae, Galleria melanella, way about a quarter of a gram
yet mount immune responses comparable to those invertebrates, so the team can test safety and effect
while cutting back on mammalian experiments.
Kuturianski said treatments that work in a different way are urgently needed as bacteria
become harder to kill with antibiotics.
And the next required step is mammalian toxicity and dosing data before any human trial.
King's College London tested KCL 286, an oral small molecule first developed for spinal cord injury
in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, according to Science Daily.
The compound activates a protein in the retinoic acid pathway, and lowered both DNA double-strand
breaks and brain inflammation.
KCL 286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety trials for its original indication.
Professor Jonathan Corcoran noted that the drug is first in class and orally bio-available,
which shortens the usual multi-year path for a new compound.
Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the development, stated that the work shows
the molecule targets DNA damage and inflammation. Two processes that appear very early in Alzheimer's
progression. The approach differs from treatments aimed mainly at amyloid beta or tau. An earlier
research had already linked disruptions in the retinoic acid pathway to amyloid beta deposits
in rat brains. mitochondrial replacement in the United Kingdom produced eight healthy burst last
year and lowered transmission of disease-causing mitochondrial mutations. Stat news reports.
parts. The technique combines genes from a mother and a father with mutation-free DNA
in the mitochondria of a donor egg. Subsequent United Kingdom data and small pilot studies
elsewhere have raised questions about whether preventing mitochondrial disease is the best
first clinical use of the method. Emerging results have prompted scientists and ethicists
to rethink potential risks and benefits before wider adoption. Regulators in Australia
are preparing their own national trial of the approach. Chinese professional masters
and PhD students in clinical medicine may soon graduate without a thesis. Nature reports.
Draft policy documents released on October 22 allow those students to submit a practical achievement
such as a clinical case analysis instead. The change follows a similar pathway introduced for
engineering students in 2024, and universities will set their own assessment standards for the new
route. Futao Huang, who studies higher education policy at Hiroshima University, said students
headed for professional careers should be trained and judged in ways that match those
careers. Joe Feifei, a spinal surgeon at Peaking University Third Hospital, said the pathway
let students be assessed on what their research will bring to patients and society. Ty Dajau
became the first to finish with a practical PhD in clinical medicine in June, after building
artificial intelligence software to help physicians classify a rare spine condition,
and leaping Dwan, chief physician of gastroenterology at the same hospital, said the hardest task
will be a uniform standard for practical work across medical fields.
Before we go, Australian regulators are preparing a national trial of mitochondrial replacement,
the next formal test of the method outside the United Kingdom.
